title: Ukraine’s remarkable anti-populism
gist: After Zelenskyy fired reformist defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov on 15 July 2026, mass protests in Kyiv and other cities forced him on 21 July to also replace Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi with Major-General Mykhailo Drapatyi. The IISS analysis argues Ukraine's binding constraint is not technology but entrenched Soviet-era military culture — micromanagement over mission command — and frames Ukraine's leaderless, disciplined, non-violent civic mobilisations of July 2025 and July 2026 as an 'anti-populism' that reliably reverses bad leadership decisions.

insights.claim: Zelenskyy replaced General Oleksandr Syrskyi with Major-General Mykhailo Drapatyi as Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on 21 July 2026, six days after firing defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: A dated leadership pivot at the top of Ukraine's war effort — the reference point for judging any subsequent change in operational tempo.
insights.locator: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's decision on 21 July 2026

insights.claim: Fedorov had been appointed only six months earlier and was Ukraine's fourth wartime defence minister, indicating extremely high turnover in the post during the war.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: Rapid ministerial churn is a structural risk to procurement continuity for defence suppliers contracting with Kyiv.

insights.claim: When Fedorov's relationship with Syrskyi broke down irreparably, Zelenskyy initially chose to retain Syrskyi over the reforming minister — a choice that mass protests then forced him to reverse.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: Zelenskyy's first instinct favoured the military establishment; street pressure, not internal deliberation, produced the reform outcome.
insights.quote: Mass protests in Kyiv and other major cities, sparked by Fedorov's sacking, have now pressured Zelenskyy into removing Syrskyi too.

insights.claim: Fedorov has reportedly been offered another government post but insists on returning as Minister of Defence, and protests look set to continue unless Zelenskyy agrees — leaving the crisis unresolved.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: Live catalyst: Fedorov's reinstatement or continued protest is the next observable checkpoint on Ukrainian domestic stability.
insights.locator: Fedorov has reportedly been offered another post

insights.claim: Drapatyi, Fedorov and Lieutenant-General Kyrylo Budanov — head of the Presidential Administration since January 2026 — together represent the post-Soviet generation and mindset the author says Ukraine needs to instil across its institutions.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: A generational cohort is now occupying the key nodes — the personnel precondition for the reform thesis to work.
insights.locator: More fundamentally, he represents, with Fedorov

themes.theme: Fedorov's reform agenda and its battlefield results

insights.claim: Fedorov drove reforms that produced a significant shift in Ukraine's military fortunes: jeopardising Russia's capacity to supply occupied Crimea, bringing the war home to ordinary Russians through fuel shortages and other effects, and inflicting higher battlefield losses.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: Ukraine's deep-strike campaign against Russian fuel logistics is credited to a specific reform agenda — its continuity depends on whether Fedorov returns.
insights.locator: Appointed only six months earlier with the boldest vision

insights.claim: The author frames the core question of Fedorov's tenure as whether a transformative agenda could prevail over resistant interests and mindset in senior Ukrainian military echelons — a bureaucratic-resistance problem rather than a resource problem.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: Aid and hardware do not resolve this bottleneck; watch senior-officer removals as the true indicator of Ukrainian military reform.
insights.quote: The question was always whether Fedorov's transformative agenda would prevail over the resistant interests and mindset in senior Ukrainian military echelons.

insights.claim: The immediate effect of Drapatyi's appointment will be on morale because, like Fedorov, he is widely respected across Ukrainian society and on the front line.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: Morale and recruitment are the near-term transmission channel — watch mobilisation and desertion data over the next quarter.
insights.locator: The effect on morale will be immediate

themes.theme: Soviet-era culture as the binding constraint

insights.claim: Ukraine leads the world in rapid wartime innovation across its defence-industry ecosystem, tactics and operations, but transformation of its military culture has been far more uneven, with best practice remaining the exception rather than the norm.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: The gap between Ukraine's hardware innovation and its command culture is the single largest untapped source of combat effectiveness.
insights.quote: While Ukraine leads the world in rapid wartime innovation in the defence-industry ecosystem, tactics and operations, transformation in its military culture has been far more uneven.
insights.locator: Rapid development, slower shift in culture

insights.claim: Three specific entrenched Soviet-era practices are named as costing lives, hurting morale and undermining recruitment and training: micromanagement rather than mission command, centralised control rather than devolved responsibility, and avoidance rather than acceptance of responsibility for failure.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: A concrete diagnostic checklist for assessing whether Ukrainian reform is real; also the template for evaluating other post-Soviet militaries.
insights.quote: micromanagement rather than mission command, centralised control rather than devolving responsibility, avoidance rather than acceptance of responsibility for failure
insights.locator: Rapid development, slower shift in culture

insights.claim: An abuse scandal that erupted in June 2026 in the Skelya regiment, which reported directly to Syrskyi, further undermined his position ahead of his removal.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: Command-accountability scandals now have removal power in Ukraine — an accountability channel that did not previously function.
insights.locator: The eruption of an abuse scandal in June

insights.claim: The author cautions that Drapatyi's appointment alone will not fix the culture problem, which requires both systemic reform and the removal of the most resistant senior officers, and depends heavily on how far Zelenskyy backs the work.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: Personnel change is necessary but not sufficient; the tell is whether senior-officer purges follow within months.
insights.quote: Culture is the hardest thing to change, and will require both systemic reform and the removal of the most resistant senior officers.
insights.locator: The appointment of Drapatyi alone will not solve this problem

insights.claim: Exactly a year before Drapatyi's appointment, Ukraine's Security Service began harassing the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) while a law was rapidly passed to strip both bodies of independence, triggering the biggest political crisis since Russia's full-scale invasion.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: Anti-corruption institutional independence is a condition of Western financing; the July 2025 episode is the precedent for how fast it can be attacked and restored.

insights.claim: Widespread demonstrations combined with diplomatic pressure from Western partners forced Ukraine's authorities to reverse the NABU/SAPO law within a week, establishing an unusually fast domestic-plus-external correction mechanism.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: Reform backsliding in Ukraine has a short half-life while both protest capacity and Western leverage persist — a positive for creditor and donor risk.

insights.claim: Andriy Yermak, previous head of the Presidential Administration and Zelenskyy's closest political ally, resigned in November 2025 after NABU and SAPO conducted searches of his home, showing the agencies reached the innermost circle.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: The credible explanation for the attack on the agencies — their investigations were reaching senior political figures — and evidence that they can force resignations.

insights.claim: The author labels Ukraine's civic mobilisation model 'anti-populism': leaderless, uniting diverse groups to hold authorities to account, a loyal opposition that criticises but rarely condemns, and disciplined, peaceful yet implacable — the inverse of populism, which inflames division, demonises elites and exploits grievances behind ambitious demagogues.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: A transferable diagnostic for distinguishing stabilising mass politics from destabilising mass politics in any country under stress.
insights.quote: It is a loyal opposition that criticises but rarely condemns. It is disciplined, peaceful, yet implacable.
insights.locator: Its modus operandi can be described as anti-populism

insights.claim: Ukrainian civil society has repeatedly shown it can organise rapidly and effectively to reverse or revise counterproductive leadership decisions despite the constraints of martial law.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: Martial law has not suppressed the correction mechanism, which lowers the tail risk of unchecked policy error in Kyiv.
insights.locator: The public mobilisations of July 2025 and July 2026

insights.claim: The author concludes that the outcomes of these mobilisations — the appointments of Budanov and Drapatyi, and perhaps Fedorov in some capacity — bode well both for the transformation of Ukraine's armed forces and for its domestic stability, arguing partners might learn from Ukraine's ability to channel grief and anger constructively in wartime.
insights.speaker: Nigel Gould-Davies
insights.so_what: The IISS read is that this crisis is stability-positive, arguing against the reflex to price Ukrainian political turbulence as regime risk.
insights.quote: Its capacity to organise with such dignity in wartime, when grief and anger might be harnessed to destructive effect, attests a maturity that its partners might learn from.
